issues.description: DEFAULT_LANGUAGE now accepts NumericLiteralSegment without a referenced spec
issues.detail: The grammar was expanded so DEFAULT_LANGUAGE = <number> parses. The PR description says only 'non-quoted identifier' is being added; the numeric branch is undocumented and not exercised by a test fixture. Either the value is essential (T-SQL allows a langid number — say so and add a test), or it is incidental — pick one. Right now the code is doing more than the PR claims.

issues.description: Negative IDENTITY seed/increment encoded as two optional SignedSegmentGrammar slots rather than as a signed numeric value
issues.detail: IDENTITY(seed, increment) takes two numbers. Numbers can be negative. The grammar now models this by gluing an optional sign in front of each NumericLiteralSegment in two places. That complects 'this token is a sign' with 'these two values are signed numbers' — the value 'a number' has been split across two parser concepts. A SignedNumericLiteralGrammar (NumericLiteralSegment optionally preceded by SignedSegmentGrammar) used once for seed and once for increment would say what's meant in one place and would compose anywhere else a signed number is allowed. Easy-not-simple.

issues.description: DROP COLUMN / DROP CONSTRAINT use nested Delimited where the inner Sequence carries IF EXISTS per-item — but the test fixture only exercises trailing IF EXISTS
issues.detail: The DROP COLUMN branch is Sequence('DROP', Delimited(Sequence('COLUMN', IfExists?, Delimited(ColumnReferenceSegment)))). The inner Delimited(ColumnReferenceSegment) inside a Delimited of Sequences allows shapes like DROP COLUMN a, b, COLUMN c that the test does not assert and that may or may not be intended T-SQL. The shape of the grammar is doing more than the documented case ('multiple delimited DROP COLUMN' where each item is COLUMN <name>). Pin the shape with a fixture, or tighten the grammar so it only accepts what's intended. Same observation for DROP CONSTRAINT.

issues.description: AlterTableStatementSegment lost its outer Delimited — confirm no legitimate comma-chained ALTER forms regress
issues.detail: Previously the whole alter body was Delimited(OneOf(...)); now it is just OneOf(...). The PR notes this as 'removed invalid delimited section' and the deleted fixture (ADD ... , DROP COLUMN ..., DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS ...) supports that claim for T-SQL. Worth a hammock minute to confirm there is no T-SQL ALTER TABLE form that legitimately chained sub-actions with commas at the top level — because the change is essentially 'the outer comma was never real T-SQL.' If true, this is a real simplification (good); if false, it's a silent regression. State the source.

review.summary: This is mostly a clean parser-grammar PR: it adds four small T-SQL surface features and deletes an invalid example. The values being parsed (signed identity seed, naked-identifier database/language, N'...' passwords, table-var indexes, delimited DROP COLUMN/CONSTRAINT) are well-scoped facts about T-SQL syntax, and pushing them into existing segments rather than inventing new ones is the simple move. Two places quietly do more than the description says: DEFAULT_LANGUAGE silently gained a numeric branch with no fixture, and the negative-identity change splits 'a signed number' across two grammar slots rather than introducing one SignedNumericLiteralGrammar value. The AlterTable restructuring removes the outer Delimited — that's a real simplification if T-SQL never allowed top-level comma chaining there, but the PR should say so explicitly rather than leaving the reader to verify. Nothing here is complected enough to block; the asks are: name what you're parsing, test what you parse, and don't let the grammar accept shapes you didn't mean.
